title: Collapse, Repair, and Drift: Dissecting Fine Tuning Dynamics in Speech Language Models

paper.title:
Collapse, Repair, and Drift:
Dissecting Fine Tuning Dynamics in Speech Language Models
paper.abstract: Abstract Supervised fine tuning (SFT) is commonly monitored through training and evaluation loss, but loss does not fully characterize how model functionality evolves along the same trajectory. We study this gap through dialect adaptation of Qwen3-ASR, MiMo-Audio, and FireRed-LLM across learning rates from 10 − 5 10^{-5} to 10 − 3 10^{-3} . Character error rate (CER) reveals pronounced transient collapse and recovery whose severity and temporal structure are only weakly reflected by loss. Bidirectional layer patching reveals strong cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse, with model dependent depth profiles that reorganize during recovery. Pairwise gradient similarity alone does not reliably indicate optimization stability, whereas raw gradient spectral analysis provides a clearer structural distinction between stable and unstable optimization: successfully converged runs approach a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, while failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or exhibit persistent fluctuations. Finally, AdamW update transfer bypasses pronounced early collapse, yet substantial Mandarin degradation still emerges later in training. These results motivate three separable SFT dynamics: collapse , repair , and drift , and show that transient collapse is not necessary for persistent source domain degradation.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Supervised fine tuning (SFT) is widely used to adapt pretrained models to new tasks and domains ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Fong et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . During training, optimization is typically monitored through training and evaluation loss, and abnormal behaviors such as loss spikes or plateaus are often used to diagnose changes in optimization dynamics ( Chang et al., 2024 ; Mircea et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . However, loss measures the optimized objective and does not directly reveal how the model’s inference-time functionality evolves along the same trajectory ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Xia et al., 2023 ) . This raises a basic question: what information about fine tuning dynamics is missed when training is characterized primarily through the loss trajectory? Speech recognition provides a useful setting for studying this question because acoustic input and textual output have strong temporal and content correspondence. Unlike open-ended tasks such as captioning, recognition errors can be localized and quantified against a well-defined reference, making functional changes easier to attribute along the training trajectory. This allows supervised loss and character error rate (CER) to provide complementary optimization and behavioral views of the same SFT process ( Radford et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . In our experiments, these two views can diverge substantially. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , evaluation loss may vary only moderately while recognition performance deteriorates sharply. We observe this behavior when adapting Qwen3-ASR ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , MiMo-Audio ( Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2025 ) , and FireRed-LLM ( Xu et al., 2025 ) to newly collected dialect speech across learning rates from 10 − 5 10^{-5} to 10 − 3 10^{-3} . Depending on the model and learning rate, CER ranges from smooth adaptation to pronounced transient collapse followed by recovery, and, at larger optimization scales, to persistent failure. To examine the transient collapse, we use bidirectional layer patching between pretrained and early SFT checkpoints. The results reveal strong and structured cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse, with model dependent depth profiles that reorganize as recognition recovers. Figure 1: Evaluation loss and recognition CER can exhibit qualitatively different trajectories during SFT. We then examine whether gradient dynamics provide a reliable description of optimization state. Successfully converged runs show characteristic within-step and inter-step cosine patterns, but similar patterns can also appear transiently earlier in training, making pairwise gradient similarity an unreliable stability indicator. In contrast, the singular value spectrum of the raw gradient matrix provides a clearer structural distinction between stable and unstable optimization. Successfully converged runs approach a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, whereas failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or exhibit persistent spectral fluctuations. Finally, we test whether early collapse is necessary for the persistent source domain degradation observed later in adaptation. Prior work has shown that abrupt performance degradation can remain recoverable ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Using AdamW update transfer, we modify the early optimization path in Qwen3-ASR at 10 − 4 10^{-4} and 10 − 5 10^{-5} and FireRed-LLM at 10 − 4 10^{-4} . In the two 10 − 4 10^{-4} settings, the intervention bypasses pronounced early collapse while gradually returning the student to ordinary SFT. Mandarin CER nevertheless subsequently drifts toward the degraded teacher regime, showing that transient collapse is not necessary for persistent source domain degradation. Taken together, these observations reveal three separable dynamics during speech model SFT: rapid collapse , subsequent repair , and slower source domain drift . Our main contributions are: • We show that severe recognition changes can be only weakly reflected in the loss trajectory, exposing transient SFT dynamics that loss alone does not characterize well. • We identify structured cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse and show that raw gradient spectral structure provides a clearer distinction between stable and unstable optimization than pairwise gradient similarity alone. • We show through AdamW update transfer that bypassing pronounced early collapse does not prevent persistent source domain degradation, separating collapse from long term drift.

sections.heading: 2.1 Speech Language Model Adaptation
sections.text: Modern speech language models connect acoustic representations to pretrained language models through speech encoders and adaptation modules. FireRed-LLM ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3-ASR ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , and MiMo-Audio ( Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2025 ) provide independently developed systems with different architectures and training recipes . We use them as complementary settings for studying SFT dynamics across models.

sections.heading: 2.2 Transient Degradation and Forgetting
sections.text: Forgetting is commonly evaluated from model performance before and after adaptation, while recent work has begun to study the trajectory itself. Spurious forgetting shows that large early performance drops can arise even when the underlying capability remains recoverable ( Zhang and Wu, 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . This motivates separating transient functional degradation from persistent capability loss, but their dynamical relationship remains unclear. We study both within the same SFT trajectory and directly intervene on the early optimization path to test whether collapse is necessary for later source domain drift.

sections.heading: 2.3 Functional and Optimization Diagnostics
sections.text: Prior studies characterize how speech and text representations are organized across LLM depth, including directional alignment and broad cross layer correspondence ( Xiang et al., 2025 ; Hsu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Glazer et al., 2026a ; Glazer et al., 2026b ) . These analyses focus on representation structure within trained models. We instead study functional compatibility across checkpoints, using bidirectional layer patching to localize how pretrained and adapted computations become incompatible during collapse and reorganize during recovery. Gradient spectra provide a complementary view of optimization structure beyond scalar loss. Spectral Lens shows that singular spectra of per sample gradients can reveal optimization changes not apparent from loss alone ( Gur-Ari et al., 2019 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . We combine pairwise gradient similarity with spectral analysis to examine whether behavioral recovery coincides with stabilization of the spectral energy distribution. Together, these lines of work motivate connecting transient behavior, functional compatibility, optimization geometry, and persistent forgetting within the same SFT trajectories.

sections.heading: 3.1 Models and Adaptation Data
sections.text: We study three independently developed LLM-based ASR models: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, MiMo-Audio-7B-Instruct, and FireRedASR2-LLM. For all models, we freeze the acoustic encoder and audio-to-language projector and fine-tune the text decoder. We adapt all models on a self-collected private speech corpus assembled for this study, covering five Chinese dialects: Changsha, Hakka, Minnan, Nanchang, and Ningbo. As the corpus is private and newly collected, it is separate from the publicly documented training data of these models. The training, validation, and test splits contain 250,000, 25,000, and 5,000 utterances, respectively. We evaluate target-domain adaptation using dialect CER and source-domain retention using Mandarin CER on 1,683 utterances from SpeechIO-3 ( Du et al., 2025 ) . Full dataset statistics and the decoding and scoring protocol are provided in Appendix A .

sections.heading: 3.2 Optimization Conditions
sections.text: For each model, we perform SFT at learning rates 10 − 5 10^{-5} , 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and 10 − 3 10^{-3} , while keeping all other optimization settings fixed within the model. We use AdamW with a constant learning rate and no warm-up in the main experiments, so that early training dynamics are observed directly under the target optimization scale. The effect of learning-rate warm-up is examined separately in Appendix F . Training runs for one full pass over the adaptation set, corresponding to T = 391 T=391 optimizer updates. Each update uses a dialect-balanced effective batch of 640 utterances, with 128 utterances from each of the five dialects. To characterize the training trajectory rather than only the endpoint, we track loss and recognition performance throughout SFT. Detailed optimization and batching configurations are provided in Appendix A.2 .

sections.heading: 4 Phenomenon: SFT Exhibits Distinct Dynamical Regimes
sections.text: Figure 2: Evaluation loss trajectories during SFT across three models and learning rates. Figure 3: Test CER curves during supervised fine-tuning across three models and learning rates on Mandarin (top) and dialect (bottom) test sets. The piecewise-linear x-axis expands steps 0–20.

sections.heading: 4.1 Loss Curves Hide Recognition Dynamics
sections.text: As shown in Fig. 2 , evaluation loss reflects the overall effect of learning rate on optimization, but provides a comparatively coarse view of the transient training trajectory. At 10 − 5 10^{-5} , loss decreases rapidly for most runs. At 10 − 3 10^{-3} , it increases early and then decreases, eventually converging to a substantially higher level than the lower learning rate runs. These curves therefore distinguish broadly successful and failed optimization regimes, but do not fully expose the severity or temporal structure of the intermediate functional changes. CER provides a more direct view of model performance. As shown in Fig. 3 , recognition can deteriorate sharply within the first few updates and then recover rapidly before entering ordinary adaptation. At 10 − 3 10^{-3} , the same early collapse is followed by only partial recovery, leaving recognition substantially worse than the base model. Thus, loss and CER broadly reflect the same training regimes, but CER makes the severity and recovery process of recognition degradation more directly observable.

sections.heading: 4.2 Model Behavior at 10 − 5 10^{-5}
sections.text: At a learning rate of 10 − 5 10^{-5} , the three models occupy different dynamical regimes. FireRed-LLM exhibits the smoothest adaptation trajectory. Dialect CER decreases from the beginning of training and gradually slows as the model approaches convergence, while Mandarin CER remains nearly unchanged. This run therefore provides a reference case in which target-domain adaptation proceeds without observable functional collapse or substantial forgetting. Qwen3-ASR and MiMo-Audio behave differently. Their dialect CER shows a mild early degradation before entering a normal convergence trajectory. Mandarin CER also deteriorates slightly at the beginning of training, then partially recovers before continuing along a gradual forgetting trajectory. These trajectories already indicate that early functional collapse, target-domain learning, and source-domain forgetting are not the same process. FireRed-LLM adapts successfully without observable collapse, whereas Qwen3-ASR and MiMo-Audio undergo a mild collapse-and-repair cycle before final convergence, accompanied by persistent but relatively stable source-domain forgetting.

sections.heading: 4.3 Model Behavior at 10 − 4 10^{-4}
sections.text: When the learning rate is increased to 10 − 4 10^{-4} , both dialect and Mandarin CER rise sharply at the beginning of training across all three models. FireRed-LLM and Qwen3-ASR then recover rapidly and proceed toward convergence. Their final dialect CER is comparable to that obtained at 10 − 5 10^{-5} , indicating that successful target-domain adaptation is still achieved. Source-domain retention is worse than at 10 − 5 10^{-5} , however: after the initial recovery, Mandarin CER remains at a persistently degraded level. Viewed from the trajectory alone, this pattern can give the impression that the later forgetting originates from the severe disruption at the beginning of training. MiMo-Audio behaves differently. After the initial CER explosion, it fails to recover into a normally convergent regime and remains substantially degraded. This behavior resembles the persistent failure observed for all three models at 10 − 3 10^{-3} .

sections.heading: 4.4 Persistent Failure at 10 − 3 10^{-3}
sections.text: At 10 − 3 10^{-3} , all three models again exhibit a sharp initial increase in both dialect and Mandarin CER. Recognition performance then remains at a high level throughout training, failing to return to the base-model performance, let alone approach the normally adapted solutions obtained at lower learning rates. Evaluation loss behaves differently: after a brief early increase, it decreases rapidly, yet its final value remains more than twice that of the normally converged lower learning rate runs. This regime is important because it distinguishes transient collapse from persistent failure. An early recovery response alone does not guarantee that the subsequent adaptation process will enter a stable training regime.

sections.heading: 5.1 Bidirectional Layer Patching
sections.text: We analyze transient functional changes during training through bidirectional layer patching between the pretrained model and early SFT checkpoints. For a model with L L LLM layers, at boundary n n we construct two hybrid models. The forward hybrid uses pretrained layers 1 1 through n n followed by SFT layers n + 1 n+1 through L L , while the reverse hybrid uses the opposite assignment. Sweeping n n produces a depthwise CER profile that measures the functional compatibility between pretrained and adapted computation. We focus on a sequence of closely spaced checkpoints around the onset, peak, and recovery of collapse. If replacing part of a degraded SFT model with pretrained layers restores recognition, the corresponding region contributes to the functional incompatibility. Reverse patching provides a complementary view by identifying where introducing SFT computation reintroduces the degraded behavior, thereby localizing the network regions associated with this incompatibility.

sections.heading: 5.2 Collapse and Repair
sections.text: As shown in Fig. 4 , all three models that undergo transient collapse and repair exhibit pronounced changes in their layer-patching profiles. However, the depthwise organization of these changes differs substantially across models. Figure 4: Bidirectional layer patching across models. Qwen3-ASR and FireRed-LLM use a learning rate of 10 − 4 10^{-4} , while MiMo-Audio uses 10 − 5 10^{-5} . The top and bottom rows show forward and reverse patching, respectively. Colored curves highlight selected checkpoints; gray curves show the remaining checkpoints. The dashed Base line in each column marks the corresponding pretrained model’s decoding CER. The patching profiles show clear functional incompatibility between partially trained checkpoints and their corresponding pretrained models. The depth at which this incompatibility is strongest varies across both models and training steps, indicating that the disruption is not confined to a fixed layer region. Comparing these profiles with the CER trajectories further shows that the step-10 checkpoints, which lie in the recovery stage, generally exhibit smoother patching curves and lower overall mismatch with the pretrained computation than checkpoints near the collapse peak. These results indicate that recoverable early collapse is associated with a highly nonuniform disruption of computation across network depth, which becomes progressively reorganized during repair.

sections.heading: 6.1 Within-Step and Inter-Step Similarity Capture Complementary Dynamics
sections.text: Figure 5 summarizes two complementary forms of gradient similarity. S intra S_{\mathrm{intra}} measures the similarity between gradients from different dialects at the same optimization step, while S inter S_{\mathrm{inter}} measures the gradient similarity of the same dialect across adjacent training steps. Under lower learning rates, runs that converge successfully generally exhibit rapid decorrelation. S intra S_{\mathrm{intra}} decreases quickly from relatively high initial similarity and then fluctuates within a narrow range around zero. As the learning rate increases, the gradients either retain stronger collinearity or exhibit substantially larger fluctuations, with the clearest deviations appearing in the failed runs at 10 − 3 10^{-3} . The inter-step similarity provides a complementary view. High S inter S_{\mathrm{inter}} can appear during early adaptation as well as in some failed high-learning-rate runs, while low S inter S_{\mathrm{inter}} can appear both transiently in early training and after successful convergence. Therefore, neither high nor low inter-step similarity alone provides a reliable indicator of convergence. Considering both within-step and inter-step similarity, successfully converged runs can be qualitatively characterized by both statistics fluctuating within a narrow range around zero. However, the gradients lie in an extremely high-dimensional parameter space, where near-orthogonality can arise naturally and cosine similarity around zero is therefore only weakly diagnostic of the underlying optimization structure. To obtain a more compact structural view, we analyze the gradient matrix through singular value decomposition and examine how its energy is distributed across the resulting singular components. Figure 5: Gradient cosine similarity across models and learning rates. Top: within-step similarity across dialects. Bottom: similarity between adjacent steps within each dialect. Colored curves show the median, shaded bands indicate the interquartile range, and gray curves show individual series.

sections.heading: 6.2 Spectral Stability Distinguishes Stable Adaptation from Unstable Optimization
sections.text: Figure 6 shows how D eff ( t ) D_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(t)} evolves during training. With five sampled gradients, 1 ≤ D eff ( t ) ≤ 5 1\leq D_{\mathrm{eff}}^{(t)}\leq 5 . Lower values indicate stronger spectral concentration, whereas values close to 5 indicate that the energy is distributed nearly uniformly across the five spectral components. For runs that converge successfully, the effective dimensionality rises rapidly during early training and then remains close to 5 for an extended period, with only minor fluctuations. In contrast, failed runs either remain highly spectrally concentrated for extended periods or exhibit persistent large fluctuations in effective dimensionality throughout training. These trajectories provide a clearer structural distinction between stable and unstable optimization than pairwise cosine similarity alone. Successful adaptation is associated with a nearly uniform and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, whereas failed optimization either remains dominated by a small number of spectral components or continues to undergo substantial spectral reorganization. The corresponding full singular-value energy distributions are provided in Appendix D.3 . Figure 6: Gradient effective dimensionality across models and learning rates, measured by D eff D_{\mathrm{eff}} . Values near 1 indicate concentrated spectral energy; values near 5 indicate approximately equal energy shares.

sections.heading: 7.1 AdamW Update Transfer Changes Early Recognition Dynamics
sections.text: We examine whether source-domain degradation still emerges when the early optimization trajectory is modified to bypass transient recognition collapse. The intervention is applied to Qwen3-ASR at learning rates of 10 − 4 10^{-4} and 10 − 5 10^{-5} and to FireRed-LLM at 10 − 4 10^{-4} . Qwen3-ASR and FireRed-LLM at 10 − 4 10^{-4} both exhibit pronounced early recognition collapse on the Mandarin and dialect test sets, whereas Qwen3-ASR at 10 − 5 10^{-5} shows only a smaller early Mandarin CER peak. sections.heading: 7.2 Long-Term Drift Persists Without Early Collapse
sections.text: Despite bypassing the early collapse, the student still exhibits source-domain degradation during subsequent training. In the teacher trajectories, Mandarin CER rises sharply, recovers rapidly, and eventually enters an approximately stable plateau. This apparent plateau can be understood as the result of continued repair of the initial collapse occurring concurrently with progressive forgetting, with the two processes partially offsetting each other. The intervention reduces the initial damage caused by collapse and therefore also reduces the amount of subsequent repair required. As the student’s own AdamW updates progressively take over, Mandarin CER rises again while dialect performance continues to improve. This exposes a long-term drift that is less masked by concurrent recovery. These results therefore separate early collapse from persistent forgetting: bypassing the former changes the temporal manifestation of source-domain degradation but does not eliminate the latter.

sections.heading: 8 Conclusion
sections.text: We studied complete SFT trajectories of Qwen3-ASR, MiMo-Audio, and FireRed-LLM across learning rates from 10 − 5 10^{-5} to 10 − 3 10^{-3} . The resulting dynamics can be organized into three separable processes: collapse , repair , and drift . Collapse corresponds to the rapid loss of recognition functionality during early adaptation, repair to the subsequent recovery from this disruption, and drift to the longer term degradation of source domain performance under continued adaptation. Their expression is strongly model and learning rate dependent: lower learning rates produce behaviors ranging from smooth adaptation to transient collapse, while larger learning rates increasingly lead to persistent recognition failure and unstable optimization. These processes are reflected at multiple levels of the training dynamics. Bidirectional layer patching associates recoverable collapse with strong cross checkpoint functional incompatibility that weakens and reorganizes during repair, with model dependent depth profiles. Gradient similarity reveals substantial changes in within-step and inter-step organization during training, but near zero cosine similarity alone is weakly diagnostic in the high dimensional parameter space. The singular value spectrum provides a more compact structural view: successfully converged runs tend toward a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, whereas failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or undergo persistent spectral reorganization. Behavioral recovery can therefore occur before the gradient spectrum reaches its later stable regime. The AdamW update transfer intervention further separates collapse from long term drift. Bypassing the early recognition collapse does not eliminate subsequent source domain degradation, indicating that persistent forgetting can emerge without the initial collapse. The intervention also suggests that the apparently stable source domain CER observed after recovery can reflect continued repair of the initial disruption occurring alongside progressive forgetting. Reducing the initial collapse reduces the amount of subsequent repair and makes the longer term drift more directly observable. Taken together, our results show that transient collapse, subsequent repair, and long term drift should be treated as distinct but interacting dynamical processes. Loss alone can obscure severe transient functional changes, pairwise gradient similarity does not uniquely characterize optimization stability, and behavioral recovery does not imply that the underlying optimization geometry has stabilized. Most importantly, the presence or absence of an early recognition collapse does not determine whether persistent source domain degradation will emerge during continued adaptation.

sections.heading: A.3 Decoding and Evaluation
sections.text: We generate transcripts autoregressively without teacher forcing, setting the maximum generation length for each utterance to twice the character length of its reference transcript. Before scoring, we extract the transcript from each model’s output and remove model-specific control tokens and metadata. We then apply Unicode NFKC normalization and lowercasing, and remove whitespace and Unicode punctuation from both references and hypotheses. For an utterance set 𝒰 \mathcal{U} , we compute corpus-level character error rate (CER), expressed as a percentage, as CER ⁡ ( 𝒰 ) = 100 ​ ∑ u ∈ 𝒰 ( S u + D u + I u ) ∑ u ∈ 𝒰 N u , \mathrm{CER}(\mathcal{U})=100\frac{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}(S_{u}+D_{u}+I_{u})}{\sum_{u\in\mathcal{U}}N_{u}}, where S u S_{u} , D u D_{u} , and I u I_{u} denote the numbers of character substitutions, deletions, and insertions under Levenshtein alignment, and N u N_{u} is the length of the normalized reference transcript. Overall dialect CER is computed by pooling errors and reference characters across all five dialects, rather than averaging dialect-specific CERs. Mandarin CER is reported separately.

sections.heading: B.3 Additional Results Across Learning Rates
sections.text: Figure 8 presents the complete bidirectional patching results for all three models at 10 − 5 10^{-5} , 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and 10 − 3 10^{-3} , extending the collapse-and-repair cases discussed in Fig. 4 . At 10 − 5 10^{-5} , the layer-patching profiles are generally smoother, especially for FireRed-LLM. As the learning rate increases, the checkpoint with the largest disruption within the first ten updates shows progressively stronger cross-checkpoint incompatibility across network depth. At 10 − 3 10^{-3} , this mismatch becomes broadly distributed across the network, with no consistent layer region capable of recovering recognition. This behavior is consistent with a transition from localized and recoverable functional disruption to near-global loss of usable pretrained computation, accompanied by persistent recognition failure and ineffective convergence. sections.heading: C.1 Gradient Extraction
sections.text: We measure dialect-specific gradients online for all nine SFT configurations. At training step t t , the gradient for dialect i i is g t , i = ∇ θ t ℒ ​ ( ℬ t , i , θ t ) , i ∈ { 1 , … , 5 } . g_{t,i}=\nabla_{\theta_{t}}\mathcal{L}(\mathcal{B}_{t,i};\theta_{t}),\qquad i\in\{1,\ldots,5\}. Here, t t indexes optimizer updates, i i indexes the five dialects, ℬ t , i \mathcal{B}_{t,i} is the batch of dialect- i i utterances used at step t t , and θ t \theta_{t} is the selected decoder parameter state immediately before that update. The loss ℒ \mathcal{L} is the cross-entropy (CE) loss computed with teacher forcing, and g t , i g_{t,i} is its gradient with respect to θ t \theta_{t} . At a full training step, each ℬ t , i \mathcal{B}_{t,i} contains 128 utterances. All five dialect gradients at step t t are measured at the same parameter state. For Qwen3-ASR and FireRed-LLM, the selected parameters comprise all trainable text-decoder components: embeddings, Transformer layers, final normalization, and the output head. For MiMo-Audio, they comprise the global text decoder and LM head, excluding local audio Transformers and audio heads. Frozen acoustic components are excluded for all models. We aggregate each dialect gradient across GPUs and accumulation micro-steps, then concatenate its parameter gradients into a single vector without layerwise normalization. These measurements are taken before gradient clipping and optimizer transformations and do not alter training. Within each model, learning-rate runs share the data sampling procedure, dialect order, and random seed. Because batches differ between steps, comparisons over time reflect both parameter changes and sampling variation.

sections.heading: Appendix E AdamW Update Transfer: Implementation
sections.text: We provide the implementation details of the AdamW update-transfer intervention described in Section 7 . The intervention is applied to Qwen3-ASR at learning rates of 10 − 4 10^{-4} and 10 − 5 10^{-5} and to FireRed-LLM at 10 − 4 10^{-4} , with all three configurations reported in Fig. 7 . All runs use seed 5230 and a constant learning rate without warm-up. Throughout this section, s s denotes the zero-based global batch-step index used in Fig. 7 . The teacher’s first ten updates therefore correspond to s = 0 , … , 9 s=0,\ldots,9 , while the pretrained checkpoint precedes s = 0 s=0 . Elsewhere in the paper, M ( 0 ) M^{(0)} denotes the pretrained checkpoint and t = 1 , … , 391 t=1,\ldots,391 counts completed optimizer updates.

sections.heading: E.1 Teacher and Student Initialization
sections.text: Teacher and student are initialized from the same pretrained checkpoint and optimize the text-decoder parameters while keeping the acoustic components frozen. The teacher follows ordinary SFT throughout the experiment. The student remains at the pretrained model parameters during global steps s = 0 , … , 9 s=0,\ldots,9 and begins updating at s start = 10 s_{\mathrm{start}}=10 . Immediately after the teacher completes its update at s = 9 s=9 , we copy the teacher’s AdamW optimizer state to the student without transferring any model parameters. For each trainable parameter, this includes the first-moment estimate, the second-moment estimate, and the optimizer step counter, which equals 10 after the first ten teacher updates. Consequently, when the student is activated at s = 10 s=10 , its model parameters remain exactly at the pretrained initialization, while its AdamW state reflects the teacher’s first ten optimization steps.

sections.text: From global step s = 10 s=10 onward, teacher and student process the same training batches of 640 utterances across eight GPUs. sections.heading: E.3 Continued Training and Evaluation
sections.text: Teacher and student continue training to the end of the same SFT epoch. After s = 70 s=70 , the student follows ordinary AdamW optimization without teacher influence or any optimizer-state reset. The uninterrupted teacher serves as the matched baseline. Checkpoints are indexed by the shared zero-based global data-stream step s s , rather than by the number of student updates since activation. We save the pretrained checkpoint, checkpoints after every indexed update from s = 0 s=0 through s = 80 s=80 , and subsequently every ten steps together with the final checkpoint. Validation loss is evaluated at these checkpoints, while CER is computed offline using the common evaluation protocol described in Appendix A.3 .

sections.heading: Appendix F Effect of Learning-Rate Warm-Up
sections.text: We examine whether learning-rate warm-up mitigates early CER degradation in three configurations: FireRed-LLM at 10 − 4 10^{-4} and Qwen3-ASR at 10 − 4 10^{-4} and 10 − 5 10^{-5} . The two 10 − 4 10^{-4} configurations exhibit pronounced early CER spikes in both domains; Qwen3-ASR at 10 − 5 10^{-5} shows early Mandarin deterioration and a dialect CER plateau. We exclude configurations with smooth adaptation or persistent optimization failure, as this experiment focuses on transient recognition degradation. For each configuration, we compare SFT without warm-up against SFT with a warm-up ratio of 0.02. During warm-up, the learning rate increases linearly to the target value and remains constant thereafter. All other training settings are unchanged. We compare test-CER trajectories on Mandarin and dialect speech. Figure 10: Test CER with and without learning-rate warm-up (warm-up ratio: 0.02). Rows show FireRed-LLM at 10 − 4 10^{-4} , Qwen3-ASR at 10 − 4 10^{-4} , and Qwen3-ASR at 10 − 5 10^{-5} , respectively. Columns show Mandarin (left) and dialect speech (right). Orange and purple curves denote runs without and with warm-up, respectively. The vertical axis is logarithmic; the horizontal axis uses different linear scales before and after step 20 to highlight early training. Figure 10 shows that the effect of warm-up depends on the model and learning rate. For FireRed-LLM at 10 − 4 10^{-4} (top row), warm-up substantially suppresses the early CER spikes on both test domains. For Qwen3-ASR at 10 − 4 10^{-4} (middle row), it delays and reduces the peaks but does not eliminate them. At 10 − 5 10^{-5} (bottom row), it delays and increases the magnitude of early Qwen3-ASR Mandarin deterioration, while dialect adaptation remains delayed. Despite these differences, runs with and without warm-up reach similar final CER on both test domains. Thus, a warm-up ratio of 0.02 does not consistently prevent early CER spikes in the tested configurations, nor does it substantially improve final Mandarin retention.

We study this gap through dialect adaptation of Qwen3-ASR, MiMo-Audio, and FireRed-LLM across learning rates from 10 − 5 10^{-5} to 10 − 3 10^{-3} . Character error rate (CER) reveals pronounced transient collapse and recovery whose severity and temporal structure are only weakly reflected by loss. Bidirectional layer patching reveals strong cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse, with model dependent depth profiles that reorganize during recovery. Pairwise gradient similarity alone does not reliably indicate optimization stability, whereas raw gradient spectral analysis provides a clearer structural distinction between stable and unstable optimization: successfully converged runs approach a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, while failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or exhibit persistent fluctuations. Finally, AdamW update transfer bypasses pronounced early collapse, yet substantial Mandarin degradation still emerges later in training. These results motivate three separable SFT dynamics: collapse , repair , and drift , and show that transient collapse is not necessary for persistent source domain degradation. 2 2 footnotetext: Equal contribution. 1 1 footnotetext: Corresponding author. 1 Introduction Supervised fine tuning (SFT) is widely used to adapt pretrained models to new tasks and domains ( Zhang et al., 2023 ; Fong et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2026 ) . During training, optimization is typically monitored through training and evaluation loss, and abnormal behaviors such as loss spikes or plateaus are often used to diagnose changes in optimization dynamics ( Chang et al., 2024 ; Mircea et al., 2025 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Luo et al., 2025 ) . However, loss measures the optimized objective and does not directly reveal how the model’s inference-time functionality evolves along the same trajectory ( Liu et al., 2023 ; Xia et al., 2023 ) . This raises a basic question: what information about fine tuning dynamics is missed when training is characterized primarily through the loss trajectory? Speech recognition provides a useful setting for studying this question because acoustic input and textual output have strong temporal and content correspondence. Unlike open-ended tasks such as captioning, recognition errors can be localized and quantified against a well-defined reference, making functional changes easier to attribute along the training trajectory. This allows supervised loss and character error rate (CER) to provide complementary optimization and behavioral views of the same SFT process ( Radford et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ) . In our experiments, these two views can diverge substantially. As illustrated in Fig. 1 , evaluation loss may vary only moderately while recognition performance deteriorates sharply. We observe this behavior when adapting Qwen3-ASR ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , MiMo-Audio ( Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2025 ) , and FireRed-LLM ( Xu et al., 2025 ) to newly collected dialect speech across learning rates from 10 − 5 10^{-5} to 10 − 3 10^{-3} . Depending on the model and learning rate, CER ranges from smooth adaptation to pronounced transient collapse followed by recovery, and, at larger optimization scales, to persistent failure. To examine the transient collapse, we use bidirectional layer patching between pretrained and early SFT checkpoints. The results reveal strong and structured cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse, with model dependent depth profiles that reorganize as recognition recovers. Figure 1: Evaluation loss and recognition CER can exhibit qualitatively different trajectories during SFT. We then examine whether gradient dynamics provide a reliable description of optimization state. Successfully converged runs show characteristic within-step and inter-step cosine patterns, but similar patterns can also appear transiently earlier in training, making pairwise gradient similarity an unreliable stability indicator. In contrast, the singular value spectrum of the raw gradient matrix provides a clearer structural distinction between stable and unstable optimization. Successfully converged runs approach a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, whereas failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or exhibit persistent spectral fluctuations. Finally, we test whether early collapse is necessary for the persistent source domain degradation observed later in adaptation. Prior work has shown that abrupt performance degradation can remain recoverable ( Zheng et al., 2025 ) . Using AdamW update transfer, we modify the early optimization path in Qwen3-ASR at 10 − 4 10^{-4} and 10 − 5 10^{-5} and FireRed-LLM at 10 − 4 10^{-4} . In the two 10 − 4 10^{-4} settings, the intervention bypasses pronounced early collapse while gradually returning the student to ordinary SFT. Mandarin CER nevertheless subsequently drifts toward the degraded teacher regime, showing that transient collapse is not necessary for persistent source domain degradation. Taken together, these observations reveal three separable dynamics during speech model SFT: rapid collapse , subsequent repair , and slower source domain drift . Our main contributions are: • We show that severe recognition changes can be only weakly reflected in the loss trajectory, exposing transient SFT dynamics that loss alone does not characterize well. • We identify structured cross checkpoint functional incompatibility during recoverable collapse and show that raw gradient spectral structure provides a clearer distinction between stable and unstable optimization than pairwise gradient similarity alone. • We show through AdamW update transfer that bypassing pronounced early collapse does not prevent persistent source domain degradation, separating collapse from long term drift. 2 Related Work 2.1 Speech Language Model Adaptation Modern speech language models connect acoustic representations to pretrained language models through speech encoders and adaptation modules. FireRed-LLM ( Xu et al., 2025 ) , Qwen3-ASR ( Shi et al., 2026 ) , and MiMo-Audio ( Xiaomi LLM-Core Team, 2025 ) provide independently developed systems with different architectures and training recipes . We use them as complementary settings for studying SFT dynamics across models. 2.2 Transient Degradation and Forgetting Forgetting is commonly evaluated from model performance before and after adaptation, while recent work has begun to study the trajectory itself. Spurious forgetting shows that large early performance drops can arise even when the underlying capability remains recoverable ( Zhang and Wu, 2024 ; Zheng et al., 2025 ) . This motivates separating transient functional degradation from persistent capability loss, but their dynamical relationship remains unclear. We study both within the same SFT trajectory and directly intervene on the early optimization path to test whether collapse is necessary for later source domain drift. 2.3 Functional and Optimization Diagnostics Prior studies characterize how speech and text representations are organized across LLM depth, including directional alignment and broad cross layer correspondence ( Xiang et al., 2025 ; Hsu et al., 2026 ; Zhang et al., 2026 ; Glazer et al., 2026a ; Glazer et al., 2026b ) . These analyses focus on representation structure within trained models. We instead study functional compatibility across checkpoints, using bidirectional layer patching to localize how pretrained and adapted computations become incompatible during collapse and reorganize during recovery. Gradient spectra provide a complementary view of optimization structure beyond scalar loss. Spectral Lens shows that singular spectra of per sample gradients can reveal optimization changes not apparent from loss alone ( Gur-Ari et al., 2019 ; Liu et al., 2026 ) . We combine pairwise gradient similarity with spectral analysis to examine whether behavioral recovery coincides with stabilization of the spectral energy distribution. Together, these lines of work motivate connecting transient behavior, functional compatibility, optimization geometry, and persistent forgetting within the same SFT trajectories. 3 Experimental Setup 3.1 Models and Adaptation Data We study three independently developed LLM-based ASR models: Qwen3-ASR-1.7B, MiMo-Audio-7B-Instruct, and FireRedASR2-LLM. The resulting dynamics can be organized into three separable processes: collapse , repair , and drift . Collapse corresponds to the rapid loss of recognition functionality during early adaptation, repair to the subsequent recovery from this disruption, and drift to the longer term degradation of source domain performance under continued adaptation. Their expression is strongly model and learning rate dependent: lower learning rates produce behaviors ranging from smooth adaptation to transient collapse, while larger learning rates increasingly lead to persistent recognition failure and unstable optimization. These processes are reflected at multiple levels of the training dynamics. Bidirectional layer patching associates recoverable collapse with strong cross checkpoint functional incompatibility that weakens and reorganizes during repair, with model dependent depth profiles. Gradient similarity reveals substantial changes in within-step and inter-step organization during training, but near zero cosine similarity alone is weakly diagnostic in the high dimensional parameter space. The singular value spectrum provides a more compact structural view: successfully converged runs tend toward a broad and temporally stable spectral energy distribution, whereas failed runs remain spectrally concentrated or undergo persistent spectral reorganization. Behavioral recovery can therefore occur before the gradient spectrum reaches its later stable regime. The AdamW update transfer intervention further separates collapse from long term drift. Bypassing the early recognition collapse does not eliminate subsequent source domain degradation, indicating that persistent forgetting can emerge without the initial collapse. The intervention also suggests that the apparently stable source domain CER observed after recovery can reflect continued repair of the initial disruption occurring alongside progressive forgetting. Reducing the initial collapse reduces the amount of subsequent repair and makes the longer term drift more directly observable. Taken together, our results show that transient collapse, subsequent repair, and long term drift should be treated as distinct but interacting dynamical processes. Loss alone can obscure severe transient functional changes, pairwise gradient similarity does not uniquely characterize optimization stability, and behavioral recovery does not imply that the underlying optimization geometry has stabilized. Most importantly, the presence or absence of an early recognition collapse does not determine whether persistent source domain degradation will emerge during continued adaptation. A.3 Decoding and Evaluation We generate transcripts autoregressively without teacher forcing, setting the maximum generation length for each utterance to twice the character length of its reference transcript. Before scoring, we extract the transcript from each model’s output and remove model-specific control tokens and metadata. We then apply Unicode NFKC normalization and lowercasing, and remove whitespace and Unicode punctuation from both references and hypotheses.
